lead: A polar plot draws the complex number G(jω) as a vector whose tip moves while ω runs from 0 to ∞. The distance from the origin is the gain |G(jω)|; the angle is the phase ∠G(jω). One curve therefore shows both quantities that a Bode plot separates. Engineers use it to see quickly how an open-loop system starts, how it ends, where it crosses the real axis, and how close it comes to the critical point −1+j0. Some syllabi call it the frequency locus.
prereq: You need 4.1 Frequency response and frequency-domain specifications and complex numbers.

blocks.text: Put s=jω in the open-loop transfer function G(s). The result G(jω) is a complex number for each frequency ω. Write it as G(jω)=X(ω)+jY(ω). X(ω) is the real part and Y(ω) is the imaginary part, both in the same units as G. The polar plot is the curve traced by the tip of the vector from the origin to X(ω)+jY(ω) while ω runs from 0 to ∞. Draw an arrow on the curve to show increasing ω.

blocks.where: X(ω) is the real part, Y(ω) is the imaginary part, |G(jω)| is the gain at frequency ω in rad/s, and ∠G(jω) is the phase angle in degrees or radians.

blocks.text: Each point carries two numbers. The distance from the origin is the magnitude |G(jω)|. The angle from the positive real axis, measured anticlockwise, is the phase ∠G(jω)=tan⁻¹(Y/X), with the quadrant chosen from the signs of X and Y. So one polar plot shows gain and phase together. A Bode plot separates them; a polar plot does not.

To sketch by hand, make a small table of ω values. For each ω compute X and Y, plot the point, and join the points smoothly. Always mark the start (ω→0⁺) and end (ω→∞); these two points identify the system type quickly.

sections.h3: Start and end points for Type 0, 1 and 2

blocks.text: Type means the number of poles of G(s) at the origin s=0. A pole at the origin is an integrator. In G(jω), a factor 1/(jω) has magnitude 1/ω and phase −90°. At ω→0⁺, 1/ω→∞. Each such pole adds −90° and makes the starting magnitude infinite.

For a proper system, the magnitude at ω→∞ is 0. The end phase is (m−n)×90°, where n is the total number of poles and m is the number of zeros. Angles that differ by 360° are the same direction. For no zeros, the end phase is −n×90°. For G(s)=1/(s(s+1)(s+2)), Type 1 starts at infinite magnitude with −90° phase and ends at the origin with +90° phase (same as −270°).

sections.h3: Crossings and what the plot tells you

blocks.text: Two crossings are easy to compute and often asked. A real-axis crossing has Im G(jω)=0. Solve that for positive ω. An imaginary-axis crossing has Re G(jω)=0. Keep only ω>0; the point ω=0 is the start.
G(jω) = 1/(a+jb) = (a − jb)/(a² + b²),   Im G(jω) = −b/(a² + b²)
blocks.where: a and b are the real and imaginary parts of the denominator at frequency ω; setting Im G = 0 means b = 0.

blocks.text: The real-axis crossing is important because the critical point is −1+j0. The distance from the curve to −1 measures how close the closed loop is to instability; gain margin and phase margin make this precise (see 4.6). For the example, Im G=0 gives ω=√2 rad/s and G=−1/6, so the curve crosses the negative real axis between 0 and −1.

Read the plot as a map of gain and phase. At low ω, the direction shows the number of integrators. At high ω, the approach to the origin shows relative degree. Near the negative real axis, the plot is close to the dangerous direction. Full encirclement and the Nyquist criterion are treated in 4.5.

figure.caption: The curve is G(s)=1/(s(s+1)(s+2)) for ω from 0.2 to 10 rad/s: it starts far down the negative imaginary axis, crosses the negative real axis at −1/6, and approaches the origin from the positive imaginary side. The distance from the origin is |G| and the angle is ∠G.

spec.aria: Polar plot starting far down the negative imaginary axis, crossing the negative real axis at −1/6, and ending at the origin from the positive imaginary side.

examples.question: Sketch the polar plot of G(s)=1/(s(s+1)(s+2)). Find its start as ω→0⁺, its end as ω→∞, and its real-axis crossing. Give the crossing frequency and the value of G there.
steps: Start: as ω→0⁺, G≈1/(j2ω)=−j/(2ω). So |G|→∞ and ∠G→−90°.
Expand: (1+jω)(2+jω)=2+3jω−ω². Multiply by jω: denominator = −3ω² + jω(2−ω²).
End: as ω→∞, denominator ≈ jω·jω·jω = −jω³. So G≈j/ω³. |G|→0 and ∠G→+90°.
Real-axis crossing: write G=1/(a+jb). Im G=−b/(a²+b²). Set b=ω(2−ω²)=0. For ω>0, ω=√2≈1.4142 rad/s.
examples.answer: The plot starts at infinite magnitude with phase −90°, ends at the origin with phase +90°, and crosses the negative real axis at ω=√2≈1.4142 rad/s with G=−1/6≈−0.1667.
examples.check:
import math
w = math.sqrt(2)
a = -3*w*w
b = w*(2 - w*w)
G = 1/complex(a, b)
print(round(w, 4))
print(round(G.real, 4))

traps: Use ω from 0 to ∞ only. Negative frequencies appear in the Nyquist plot, not in the standard polar plot.
A pole at the origin makes the start magnitude infinite. Do not start at a finite point and do not draw a closed loop back to the start.
When solving Im G=0, use G=1/(a+jb)=(a−jb)/(a²+b²); the imaginary part is −b/(a²+b²), not +b.
Type is not the same as order. Type counts only poles at the origin; order counts all poles of G(s).
Phase can be written as +90° or −270°. The direction is the same; do not call it a different curve.

quiz.q: On a polar plot, what do the radius and angle at a point represent?
Which range of ω is plotted in a polar plot?
Why does a Type 1 system start at infinite magnitude and −90° phase?
quiz.a: The pole at origin gives factor 1/(jω): magnitude 1/ω→∞ as ω→0⁺, phase −90°.

quiz.q: For G(s)=1/(s(s+1)(s+2)), find the real-axis crossing frequency and the value of G there.
quiz.a: G(jω)=1/[−3ω²+jω(2−ω²)]. Set imaginary part zero: 2−ω²=0, ω=√2≈1.414 rad/s. Then G=−1/6≈−0.1667.

quiz.q: For G(jω)=1/(jω(1+jω)), find the start phase and the end phase.
quiz.a: Start: Type 1, ω→0⁺, G≈1/(jω), phase −90°. End: denominator order 2, phase →−180° (same as +180°).

quiz.q: A polar plot starts finite on the positive real axis and ends at the origin with phase −270°. What type and total number of poles can you infer?
quiz.a: Finite start means Type 0. End phase −270° ≡ +90°, so with no zeros the total denominator order n satisfies −n×90°=−270°, n=3. So Type 0, order 3.

quiz.q: The polar plot of G(s)=K/(s(s+1)(s+2)) crosses the negative real axis at −K/6. Find K for the crossing to pass through −1.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, polar plots are used in relay auto-tuning and in servo loop commissioning, where a technician checks the phase at the gain crossover. Modern software draws the same locus from measured frequency response data. Search for polar plot of measured frequency response, and for frequency locus in robust control. The idea extends to the Nyquist contour and to describing functions for nonlinear systems.
